title: Regression Metrics
abstract:
Seven metrics, in three families. MAE, MSE and RMSE say how wrong the model
is in absolute terms — the error size in the target's own units.
$R^2$ and Adjusted $R^2$ say how good the model is — how much of the
variation in the data it explains. MAPE and WMAPE say how wrong the prediction is
in business terms. This document gives every formula, what each metric is
robust or vulnerable to, the derivation of why $R^2$ always rises when a feature
is added and how the adjustment fixes it, and the rule for choosing which to
report.

items:
MAE, MSE, RMSE — predict how wrong the model is in
 absolute terms (error size in units).

$R^2$ & Adjusted $R^2$ — measure or tell how good the
 model is; they explain the variation in the data.

MAPE, WMAPE — measure how wrong the prediction is
 in business terms.

blocks.t:
Throughout: $y_i$ is the actual value, $\hat y_i$ the predicted value, and $n$ the
number of data points.

rows: Error is in the same unit as the target — "we are off by 4.2 minutes" is directly meaningful. Robust to outliers.
Uses a modulus, so it can't be differentiated at zero — which makes it awkward as a training loss.

blocks.t:
The constant that minimises MAE is the median. So a model trained on MAE
predicts the conditional median of $y$, not the conditional mean. On a skewed
target those are different numbers, and which one the business wants is a real
decision.

blocks.cap:
Left: the penalty shapes. Middle: their gradients — MAE's is a step
 with a discontinuity at zero, which is exactly why it cannot be used directly
 with the closed-form or standard gradient methods. Right: with one outlier
 present, MSE's optimum is dragged towards it while MAE's stays at the median.

rows: Uses a square, so it is differentiable — and can therefore be used as a loss function.
Can't handle outliers well — the square makes a single large error dominate. And the unit differs from the target (rupees$^2$, minutes$^2$), so the number is not interpretable.

blocks.t: MSE has a decomposition no other metric has:

This is the formal basis of Topic 40, and it is one reason MSE is the default
theoretical object even when MAE is the better thing to report.

rows: Same properties as MSE — differentiable, outlier-sensitive — but it has the same unit as the target.

blocks.t: RMSE vs MAE: the gap is a diagnostic

$\text{RMSE}\ge\text{MAE}$ always, with equality only when every error has the
same magnitude. The ratio tells you about the error distribution:

items: $\text{RMSE}\approx\text{MAE}$: errors are uniform in size.

$\text{RMSE}\gg\text{MAE}$: a few very large errors dominate — go and
 look at them.

blocks.t: Reporting both is more informative than reporting either alone.

It essentially tells by how much the predicted line deviates from the
mean line.
$R^2$ close to 1 means good model performance.

blocks.cap:
$R^2$ is a comparison against a baseline. $SS_{\text{mean}}$ is the
 error you would make by always predicting $\bar y$; $SS_{\text{reg}}$ is the
 error your model actually makes. $R^2$ is the fraction of the baseline error
 you removed.

rows: Perfect — every point on the line
The model explains 70% of the variance in $y$
No better than always predicting the mean
Worse than the mean. Possible on a test set, and a sign of a badly broken model

blocks.t: Three things $R^2$ does not tell you

items:
It is unitless and relative. $R^2=0.9$ on an easy target may be
 worse in business terms than $R^2=0.3$ on a hard one.

It does not indicate a good fit. Anscombe's quartet is four
 datasets with identical $R^2$ and completely different shapes — one is a
 parabola, one is driven by a single outlier. Always plot the residuals.

It always increases when you add a feature. Which is the next
 section.

blocks.t:
$R^2$ always increases when we add new features, even if the new features
add no value. Adjusted $R^2$ penalises extra features and increases only
when a new variable truly improves the model.

where $n$ is the number of rows and $k$ the independent column count — the
number of predictors.

Adding a column enlarges the column space of $X$ to a superset. Least squares
finds the closest point in that space to $y$, so the minimum achievable
$SS_{\text{reg}}$ over a larger space can only be smaller or equal.
Formally, the old solution is still available — set the new coefficient to zero
— so the optimiser can never do worse. Since $SS_{\text{mean}}$ is unchanged,
$R^2$ can only rise.

Adjusted $R^2$ divides $SS_{\text{reg}}$ by $n-1-k$ instead of $n-1$. Adding a
useless feature shrinks the numerator by a negligible amount but shrinks the
denominator by one, so the ratio rises and $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ falls. It
increases only when the reduction in error outweighs the degree of freedom spent.

blocks.cap:
Left: 60 rows, three genuine features, the rest pure noise. $R^2$
 climbs monotonically to 1 — a perfect fit to random numbers — while
 adjusted $R^2$ peaks near the true feature count and then collapses. Right:
 why MAPE and WMAPE differ.

blocks.t: On average, by how much % the prediction is wrong.
Error in prediction % for business. Lower MAPE or WMAPE is good.

MAPE divides each error by its own actual value, so a tiny actual
produces an enormous percentage. Forecasting 1 unit when 2 sold is a 50% error;
forecasting 1000 when 1010 sold is a 1% error — yet the second miss is ten
units and the first is one. MAPE weights the trivial SKU as heavily as the
important one.

WMAPE divides the total absolute error by the total actual, so each
error is implicitly weighted by its size. It is the standard demand-forecasting
metric for exactly this reason.

items:
Undefined at $\text{actual}=0$ — division by zero. Common in
 intermittent demand.

Asymmetric. Over-forecasting is unbounded (error can exceed
 100%) while under-forecasting is capped at 100%. A model optimised on
 MAPE learns to under-forecast systematically.
Dominated by small actuals, as above.

Unit
Outliers
Report it when
rows: You want an interpretable typical error
You are training, or decomposing bias/variance
Explaining the model's share of variance
Comparing models with different feature counts
Scale-free comparison, no zeros, similar magnitudes
Demand forecasting and any business % error

blocks.t:
Any of these numbers is meaningless alone. Report it beside the same metric for a
trivial model — predict the mean, or predict last month's value. A RMSE of 12
is excellent or terrible depending entirely on what predicting $\bar y$ would
have scored.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error,
                             r2_score, mean_absolute_percentage_error)
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, (n, 1))
y = 3 * x.ravel() + 5 + rng.normal(0, 2, n)
model = LinearRegression().fit(x, y)
pred = model.predict(x)

# =====================================================================
# 1. EVERY FORMULA, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
err = y - pred
mae  = np.abs(err).mean()
mse  = (err ** 2).mean()
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
r2   = 1 - np.sum(err**2) / np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
k    = x.shape[1]
r2a  = 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - 1 - k)
mape = np.mean(np.abs(err / y)) * 100
wmape = np.sum(np.abs(err)) / np.sum(y) * 100

print(f"MAE   {mae:8.4f}   sklearn {mean_absolute_error(y, pred):8.4f}")
print(f"MSE   {mse:8.4f}   sklearn {mean_squared_error(y, pred):8.4f}")
print(f"RMSE  {rmse:8.4f}   sklearn {mean_squared_error(y, pred)**.5:8.4f}")
print(f"R2    {r2:8.4f}   sklearn {r2_score(y, pred):8.4f}")
print(f"AdjR2 {r2a:8.4f}")
print(f"MAPE  {mape:8.4f}%  sklearn "
      f"{mean_absolute_percentage_error(y, pred)*100:8.4f}%")
print(f"WMAPE {wmape:8.4f}%")

# =====================================================================
# 2. RMSE >= MAE ALWAYS -- and the ratio is a diagnostic
# =====================================================================
uniform = rng.normal(0, 2, 400)                       # all errors similar
spiky   = np.r_[rng.normal(0, .4, 396), [22., -20., 25., -24.]]  # a few huge
for name, e in [("uniform errors", uniform), ("a few huge errors", spiky)]:
    a, r = np.abs(e).mean(), np.sqrt((e**2).mean())
    print(f"{name:20s} MAE {a:6.2f}  RMSE {r:6.2f}  ratio {r/a:5.2f}")
# ratio ~1.25 = uniform;  ratio > 3 = go and look at the tail.

# =====================================================================
# 3. MAE IS ROBUST, MSE IS NOT
# =====================================================================
y_out    = y.copy();    y_out[:5] += 60               # 1% of rows corrupted
pred_out = LinearRegression().fit(x, y_out).predict(x)
print(f"\n{'':14s} {'clean':>10s} {'1% corrupted':>14s}")
print(f"{'MAE':14s} {mean_absolute_error(y, pred):10.3f} "
      f"{mean_absolute_error(y_out, pred_out):14.3f}")
print(f"{'RMSE':14s} {mean_squared_error(y, pred)**.5:10.3f} "
      f"{mean_squared_error(y_out, pred_out)**.5:14.3f}")
# RMSE roughly doubles; MAE moves far less.

# WHAT EACH ONE OPTIMISES: mean vs median
z = np.r_[rng.normal(0, 1, 300), [12.]]
grid = np.linspace(-1, 12, 2000)
print(f"\nMSE-optimal constant {grid[np.argmin([(np.mean((z-g)**2)) for g in grid])]:.3f} "
      f"(mean {z.mean():.3f})")
print(f"MAE-optimal constant {grid[np.argmin([(np.mean(np.abs(z-g))) for g in grid])]:.3f} "
      f"(median {np.median(z):.3f})")

# =====================================================================
# 4. R2 ALWAYS RISES; ADJUSTED R2 DOES NOT
# =====================================================================
m = 60
Xs = rng.normal(0, 1, (m, 3))
ys = Xs @ [2, -1, .5] + rng.normal(0, 1, m)

print(f"\n{'features':>9s} {'R2':>8s} {'AdjR2':>8s}")
for kk in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40, 55]:
    Xk = np.c_[Xs, rng.normal(0, 1, (m, max(kk-3, 0)))][:, :kk]
    p_ = LinearRegression().fit(Xk, ys).predict(Xk)
    r  = r2_score(ys, p_)
    ra = 1 - (1 - r) * (m - 1) / (m - 1 - kk)
    print(f"{kk:9d} {r:8.4f} {ra:8.4f}")
# Only the first 3 features are real. R2 climbs to 1.0 (a perfect fit to
# noise); adjusted R2 peaks near 3 and then collapses.

# R2 CAN BE NEGATIVE on held-out data:
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(Xs, ys, test_size=.4, random_state=0)
bad = LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[X_tr, rng.normal(0,1,(len(X_tr),30))], y_tr)
print("\ntest R2 of an overfitted model:",
      round(r2_score(y_te, bad.predict(np.c_[X_te, rng.normal(0,1,(len(X_te),30))])), 3))
# Negative means WORSE than predicting the mean.

# =====================================================================
# 5. MAPE vs WMAPE -- the demand-forecasting case
# =====================================================================
actual = np.array([   2,    3,    1, 1000, 1200,  950])   # 3 tiny, 3 large SKUs
predic = np.array([   1,    5,    2, 1010, 1180,  960])

per_item = np.abs((actual - predic) / actual) * 100
print("\nper-item % error:", per_item.round(1))
print(f"MAPE  {per_item.mean():6.2f}%   <- dominated by the three tiny SKUs")
print(f"WMAPE {np.sum(np.abs(actual-predic))/np.sum(actual)*100:6.2f}%   "
      f"<- weighted by volume, which is what the business feels")
print(f"total units mis-forecast: {np.abs(actual-predic).sum()} of {actual.sum()}")

# MAPE IS UNDEFINED AT ZERO:
with_zero = np.array([0., 5., 10.])
print("\nMAPE with a zero actual:",
      np.mean(np.abs((with_zero - np.array([1., 5., 9.])) /
                     np.where(with_zero == 0, np.nan, with_zero))))
print("WMAPE handles it:",
      round(np.sum(np.abs(with_zero - np.array([1.,5.,9.])))/np.sum(with_zero)*100, 2), "%")

# MAPE IS ASYMMETRIC -- which teaches a model to under-forecast:
a = np.array([100.])
print(f"\nover-forecast by 50:  MAPE {abs((a-150)/a)[0]*100:.0f}%")
print(f"under-forecast by 50: MAPE {abs((a-50)/a)[0]*100:.0f}%")
print("over-forecast by 500: MAPE", f"{abs((a-600)/a)[0]*100:.0f}%",
      "-- unbounded above, capped at 100% below")

# =====================================================================
# 6. ALWAYS COMPARE AGAINST A BASELINE
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
base = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
mdl  = LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\n{'':10s} {'baseline':>10s} {'model':>10s} {'improvement':>13s}")
for name, fn in [("MAE",  mean_absolute_error),
                 ("RMSE", lambda a_, b_: mean_squared_error(a_, b_) ** .5)]:
    bl = fn(y_te, base.predict(X_te)); md = fn(y_te, mdl.predict(X_te))
    print(f"{name:10s} {bl:10.3f} {md:10.3f} {1-md/bl:12.1%}")
print(f"{'R2':10s} {r2_score(y_te, base.predict(X_te)):10.3f} "
      f"{r2_score(y_te, mdl.predict(X_te)):10.3f}")
# An RMSE of 2.0 means nothing until you know the baseline scored 8.7.
Every regression metric on one set of predictions
R$^2$ and adjusted R$^2$. Mean of $y$ is $4.25$. $SS_{\text{tot}} = 14.75$, $SS_{\text{res}} = 5.25$:
Adjusted R$^2$ is lower because the sample is tiny: the penalty for the number of rows is large when $n-p-1$ is small.

Which to report. MAE is in the target's units and robust to outliers. RMSE punishes the single error of $-2$ more heavily than the rest. MAPE breaks when any $y_i=0$. WMAPE avoids that by dividing the total absolute error by the total of $y$.

items:
MAE, MSE, RMSE tell you how wrong the model is in
 absolute terms. $R^2$, Adjusted $R^2$ tell you how good
 the model is. MAPE, WMAPE express the error in business
 terms.

$\text{MAE}=\sum\frac{|y_i-\hat y_i|}{n}$. Advantages: same unit
 as the target, robust to outliers. Disadvantage: uses a modulus,
 so it cannot be differentiated.

$\text{MSE}=\sum\frac{(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{n}$. Advantage: uses a square,
 so it is differentiable and can be used as a loss function.
 Disadvantages: cannot handle outliers well, and the
 unit differs from the target.

$\text{RMSE}=\sqrt{\text{MSE}}$ — same properties as MSE but the
 same unit as the target. $\text{RMSE}\ge\text{MAE}$ always; a
 large ratio means a few huge errors.

$R^2$ always increases when a feature is added, because the
 column space only grows. Adjusted $R^2$ penalises extra features:
 $R^2_{\text{adj}}=1-\frac{(1-R^2)(n-1)}{n-1-k}$, with $n$ rows and $k$
 predictors.

$\text{MAPE}=\frac1n\sum\left|\frac{A-P}{A}\right|\times100$ — on
 average, by how much % the prediction is wrong. Undefined at zero,
 asymmetric, dominated by small actuals.

$\text{WMAPE}=\frac{\sum|A-P|}{\sum A}\times100$ — weights each error by
 its size. Lower MAPE or WMAPE is good.
Every metric is meaningless without a baseline.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked

MAE when you want an interpretable typical error and outliers should not dominate.
RMSE when large errors are disproportionately costly — an ETA that is 40 minutes
wrong is far worse than four that are 10 minutes wrong. Report both: the ratio
tells you whether the errors are uniform or driven by a few extremes.
Q. Why is MSE used as a loss function but MAE reported as a metric?

MSE is differentiable everywhere, which is what closed-form and gradient-based
optimisation require; MAE has a kink at zero. But MSE is in squared units, so it
is meaningless to a stakeholder — MAE or RMSE is what you report.
Q. Why does $R^2$ always increase when you add a feature?

Because least squares minimises over a larger column space, and the previous
solution is still available (set the new coefficient to zero). The minimum error
can only fall, and $SS_{\text{mean}}$ is unchanged. Adjusted $R^2$ divides by
$n-1-k$, so a useless feature costs a degree of freedom and lowers the score.

Yes, on held-out data. It means the model is worse than always predicting the
training mean — typically severe overfitting, or a target distribution that
shifted between train and test.
Q. Your demand forecast has MAPE 45% but WMAPE 6%. What is going on?

The large percentage errors are concentrated on low-volume SKUs, where a
one-unit miss is a huge percentage. WMAPE weights by volume, so it reflects what
the business actually feels. Report WMAPE, and if the small SKUs genuinely matter,
report their error separately rather than letting them distort the headline.
Q. Why does optimising MAPE make a model under-forecast?

Because MAPE is asymmetric: under-forecasting caps at 100% error while
over-forecasting is unbounded. The optimiser learns that predicting low is safer,
which systematically biases the forecast downward.

Not established. $R^2$ says nothing about whether the functional form is right —
Anscombe's quartet gives four wildly different datasets identical $R^2$. Check the
residual plot for structure, check the error in business units, and compare
against a baseline.
